jhmt-2020-ms-long-04.title: Set up equation
jhmt-2020-ms-long-04.body: Let sister's age be $x$, so Steve's is $2x$. In 6 years: $(2x+6)+(x+6) = 36$. So $3x = 24$, $x = 8$. Steve's age: $2(8) = \boxed{16}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-long-05.title: Maximize and minimize overlaps
jhmt-2020-ms-long-05.body: Randy fails 3 exams and 2 homeworks. **Maximum passes:** concentrate failures — if the 2 homework failures are among the 3 exam failures, he fails at most 3 classes and passes 2. **Minimum passes:** spread failures — if each of the 5 classes has at least one failure, he passes 0. Difference: $2 - 0 = \boxed{2}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-long-06.title: Diagonal vs perimeter path
jhmt-2020-ms-long-06.body: Aaron's diagonal: $\sqrt{8^2+6^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ m. Tim's path around two sides: $8+6 = 14$ m. Difference: $14-10 = \boxed{4}$ m.

jhmt-2020-ms-long-07.title: Solve for angle
jhmt-2020-ms-long-07.body: Let the angle be $x$. Its complement is $90°-x$. Given: $90°-x = x+40°$, so $2x = 50°$, $x = 25°$. Supplement: $180°-25° = \boxed{155°}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-long-08.title: Pair consecutive terms
jhmt-2020-ms-long-08.body: Group into pairs: $(-1+2)+(-3+4)+\cdots+(-2019+2020)$. Each pair sums to $1$, and there are $2020/2 = 1010$ pairs. Sum $= \boxed{1010}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-long-09.title: Pythagorean triple
jhmt-2020-ms-long-09.body: $a^2+b^2 = 289$. Try $a \le b$; since $2b^2 \ge 289$ gives $b \ge 12$. Check $b=15$: $a^2 = 289-225 = 64$, $a=8$. The only solution (up to order) is $(a,b)=(8,15)$, giving $a+b = \boxed{23}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-long-10.title: Doubling formula
jhmt-2020-ms-long-10.body: After $n$ doublings, he has $300 \cdot 2^n$ gold. We need $300 \cdot 2^n \ge 1{,}000{,}000$, i.e.~$2^n \ge 3334$. Since $2^{12} = 4096 > 3334 > 2048 = 2^{11}$, he needs $n=12$ doublings, taking $12 \times 2 = \boxed{24}$ days.

jhmt-2020-ms-long-11.title: Eliminate x
jhmt-2020-ms-long-11.body: Multiply the first equation by 3 and add to the second: $(3+a)x = 75$. For no solution, the $x$ coefficient must be 0: $3+a = 0$, giving $a = \boxed{-3}$ (which makes the second equation $0=75$, indeed inconsistent).

jhmt-2020-ms-long-12.title: Identify valid configuration
jhmt-2020-ms-long-12.body: If the equal sides were 18, the triangle inequality $18+18 > 41$ would fail ($36 < 41$). So the equal sides must be 41, with base 18. The height from the base is $h = \sqrt{41^2 - 9^2} = \sqrt{1681-81} = \sqrt{1600} = 40$. Area $= \frac{1}{2}(18)(40) = \boxed{360}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-long-13.title: Areas of regular hexagon and equilateral triangle
jhmt-2020-ms-long-13.body: Hexagon area: $\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}s^2 = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}(64) = 96\sqrt{3}$. Triangle area: $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(256) = 64\sqrt{3}$. Ratio: $\frac{96\sqrt{3}}{64\sqrt{3}} = \frac{3}{2}$. So $a+b = 3+2 = \boxed{5}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-long-15.title: Geometric probability
jhmt-2020-ms-long-15.body: Probability of hitting the board: $\frac{4}{5}$. Given on the board, probability of missing bulls-eye: $\frac{9\pi - \pi}{9\pi} = \frac{8}{9}$. Combined: $\frac{4}{5} \times \frac{8}{9} = \frac{32}{45}$. So $a+b = 32+45 = \boxed{77}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-long-16.title: Solve the equation
jhmt-2020-ms-long-16.body: Multiply by $11b(11+b)$: $44b = b(11+b) + 11(11+b) = 11b + b^2 + 121 + 11b$. So $b^2 - 22b + 121 = 0$, i.e.~$(b-11)^2 = 0$. The only solution is $b = 11$. Sum of all values: $\boxed{11}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-long-17.title: Inscribed square
jhmt-2020-ms-long-17.body: The four points are equally spaced on the circle (each arc is $\frac{1}{4}$ of the circle), forming an inscribed square. The circle has area $2\pi$, so $\pi r^2 = 2\pi$ gives $r = \sqrt{2}$. The inscribed square has diagonal $2r = 2\sqrt{2}$, so side $= 2$, area $= \boxed{4}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-long-18.title: Factor count formula
jhmt-2020-ms-long-18.body:
If $n=p_1^{e_1}\cdots p_k^{e_k}$, then $n$ has $(e_1+1)\cdots(e_k+1)$ factors, so we need this product to be $20$. The ways to write $20$ as a product of factors greater than $1$ are $20$, $10\cdot2$, $5\cdot4$, $5\cdot2\cdot2$. Giving the largest exponents to the smallest primes, the candidates are
$$2^{19},\quad 2^9\cdot3=1536,\quad 2^4\cdot3^3=432,\quad 2^4\cdot3\cdot5=240.$$
The smallest is $\boxed{240}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-long-19.title: Set up equation
jhmt-2020-ms-long-19.body: Initial water: $0.95 \times 2 = 1.9$ kg. Add $x$ kg water: $\frac{1.9+x}{2+x} = 0.99$. So $1.9+x = 1.98+0.99x$, giving $0.01x = 0.08$, $x = \boxed{8}$ kg.

jhmt-2020-ms-long-20.title: Count valid outcomes
jhmt-2020-ms-long-20.body: $36 = 2^2 \times 3^2$. Valid unordered triples from $\{1,...,6\}$: $(1,6,6)$, $(2,3,6)$, $(4,3,3)$. Ordered counts: $3+6+3 = 12$. Total outcomes: $6^3 = 216$. Probability: $\frac{12}{216} = \frac{1}{18}$. So $a+b = 1+18 = \boxed{19}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-long-21.title: Overlap is a quarter of the small square
jhmt-2020-ms-long-21.body:
Let $C$ be the center of Desmonida; Erida has a vertex at $C$ and its two sides from $C$ make a right angle. Since Erida's sides ($15$) are longer than the distance from $C$ to any point of Desmonida (at most $5\sqrt2<15$), the overlap is exactly the part of Desmonida inside that right angle at $C$.

Draw the two lines through $C$ parallel to Desmonida's sides; they cut Desmonida into four $5\times5$ squares. Rotating the right angle by $30^\circ$ away from one of these quarter squares removes a right triangle from one side of that quarter and adds a congruent right triangle on the other side: both are right triangles with a leg of $5$ (from $C$ to the side of Desmonida) and the angle $30^\circ$ at $C$. So the overlap has the same area as one quarter square, $5^2=\boxed{25}$ square miles (for any rotation angle).

jhmt-2020-ms-long-22.title: Solve for bill counts
jhmt-2020-ms-long-22.body:
Ryan has at least one \$50 bill, so the other $45$ bills total \$61. A second \$50 would leave \$11 for $44$ bills, and a \$20 would leave \$41 for $44$ bills; both are impossible since each bill is worth at least \$1. With $t$ ten-dollar bills, $f$ fives and $o$ ones: $t+f+o=45$ and $10t+5f+o=61$; subtracting, $9t+4f=16$, so $t=0$ (since $t=1$ gives $4f=7$) and $f=4$, $o=41$.

So $4$ of the $46$ bills are \$5 bills, the probability is $\frac{4}{46}=\frac{2}{23}$, and $a+b=2+23=\boxed{25}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-long-23.title: Regions formula
jhmt-2020-ms-long-23.body: Adding the $k$th line to $k-1$ existing lines (with no two parallel, no three concurrent) adds exactly $k$ new regions. Starting from 1 region: $1 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = \boxed{16}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-long-24.title: Identify integer bounds
jhmt-2020-ms-long-24.body: $-4\sqrt{5} = -\sqrt{80} \approx -8.94$, so the smallest integer above it is $-8$. $3\sqrt[3]{9} = \sqrt[3]{243} \approx 6.24$, so the largest integer below it is $6$. Sum from $-8$ to $6$: $\frac{(-8+6)(15)}{2} = \frac{(-2)(15)}{2} = \boxed{-15}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-long-25.title: Split prime factors
jhmt-2020-ms-long-25.body: The primes up to 25 are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 — nine primes. For $\gcd(a,b) = 1$, each prime power factor of $25!$ must go entirely to $a$ or entirely to $b$. So there are $2^9 = \boxed{512}$ ordered pairs $(a,b)$.

jhmt-2020-ms-long-26.title: Divisibility by 4, 3 and 11
jhmt-2020-ms-long-26.body:
Since $132=4\cdot3\cdot11$, the number $1a4b4c$ must be divisible by each of $4$, $3$, $11$.

- **By 11:** the alternating sum $1-a+4-b+4-c=9-(a+b+c)$ is a multiple of $11$. As $0\le a+b+c\le27$, $a+b+c\in\{9,20\}$.
- **By 3:** the digit sum $9+a+b+c$ is a multiple of $3$, so $3\mid a+b+c$. Hence $a+b+c=9$.
- **By 4:** the last two digits $\overline{4c}$ are divisible by $4$, so $c\in\{0,4,8\}$.

If $c=0$ the product is $0$. If $c=8$, then $a+b=1$, so $a$ or $b$ is $0$. If $c=4$, then $a+b=5$ and $ab$ is at most $2\cdot3=6$. The largest product is $2\cdot3\cdot4=\boxed{24}$ (e.g. $124344=132\cdot942$).

jhmt-2020-ms-long-27.title: Euler path analysis
jhmt-2020-ms-long-27.body:
In the combined figure, each octahedron vertex other than the shared one has degree $4$, each tetrahedron vertex other than the shared one has degree $3$, and the shared vertex has degree $4+3=7$. So there are $4$ odd-degree vertices: the shared vertex and the three other tetrahedron vertices.

A walk that uses every edge exactly once can have at most $2$ odd-degree vertices (its start and end), so Rob must repeat at least one edge: at least $19$. Repeating one edge between two non-shared tetrahedron vertices leaves exactly two odd vertices, the shared vertex (the start) and the third tetrahedron vertex, so a walk of length $19$ exists. Concretely, Rob first traverses all $12$ octahedron edges in a closed loop (every octahedron vertex has even degree), returns to the shared vertex, and then covers the tetrahedron in $7$ edges, e.g. $S\to P\to Q\to R\to S\to Q\to P\to R$ with $S$ shared.

The minimum distance is $12+7=\boxed{19}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-long-28.title: Factor
jhmt-2020-ms-long-28.body: $abc + ab + ac + bc + a + b + c = (a+1)(b+1)(c+1) - 1 = 1000$, so $(a+1)(b+1)(c+1) = 1001 = 7 \times 11 \times 13$. With $a,b,c \ge 1$, each factor is $\ge 2$. The only factorization of 1001 into three factors $\ge 2$ is $\{7,11,13\}$. The ordered triplets $(a+1,b+1,c+1)$ are the $3! = 6$ permutations, giving $6$ ordered triplets $(a,b,c)$. $\boxed{6}$.
